snippet.title: Why No One Smiled in Old Photos  #history  #art
snippet.description:
In the 1800s, cameras needed 20 seconds to take a single photo. If you moved even slightly… the picture would blur.

So Victorian photographers used hidden iron stands with claws. Clamped to the back of the head or waist. Then hidden under dresses or curtains.

That's why no one smiled in old photos. Not because they were sad. Because they were clamped.

snippet.title: The Rise and Fall of the Vikings | Why the Most Feared Warriors in History Vanished
snippet.description:
For centuries, the Vikings struck fear across Europe raiding coasts, exploring new lands, and building a reputation as some of the most formidable warriors in history. But over time, their dominance faded.

In this video, we explore the rise, expansion, and eventual decline of the Viking world, and what really caused their disappearance as a major force.

You’ll Discover:
How Viking society and seafaring skills fueled their rapid expansion
The role of trade, exploration, and settlement beyond raiding
Why European defenses and kingdoms became harder to attack
The impact of Christianization and cultural change
How political shifts and integration led to the end of the Viking Age

The Vikings didn’t just vanish overnight they evolved, settled, and became part of the societies they once raided.

Sometimes the end of an era… isn’t destruction, but transformation.

snippet.title: Google Just Killed Websites. It's Not Good.
snippet.description:
Google built the internet by sending people to websites. Now it's doing the opposite.

AI-powered search results are answering questions before users ever click a link, keeping traffic inside Google's ecosystem while the websites that created the information lose visitors, revenue, and sometimes their entire business. Independent publishers, review sites, and niche experts are watching years of work disappear as AI Overviews replace the clicks they once depended on.

In this video, we explore how Google's AI search revolution is reshaping the web, why millions of searches now end without visiting a single website, how Reddit became one of the biggest winners, and why many experts believe the open internet is entering a dangerous new phase.
The company that once organized the web may now be consuming it.

If Google keeps readers and websites lose their audience, what happens when there’s nobody left creating the knowledge AI depends on?

snippet.title: 1315: The Great Famine — When Villages Chose Who Lived and Died
snippet.description:
A year of hunger. A collapsing society. And villages forced to make impossible decisions.

In 1315, Europe was struck by one of the worst famines in its history. Crops failed, rains never stopped, and entire communities were pushed to the edge of survival. As food disappeared, morality collapsed — and survival meant making choices no one should ever have to face.

This video respectfully explores the Great Famine of 1315–1317, a devastating period when starvation reshaped medieval society and forced villages into brutal decisions about life and death.

In this video, discover how:

• Endless rain destroyed harvests across Northern Europe
• Food shortages quickly turned into mass starvation
• Entire villages struggled to survive through the winter
• Social order collapsed under extreme hunger
• Survival sometimes meant deciding who would eat — and who would not

What would you do when there is not enough food for everyone? Share your thoughts in the comments, and subscribe for more true stories from medieval history, survival, and human endurance.

snippet.title: Why Did Snipers Wear Diapers in Vietnam War?
snippet.description:
Why did Vietnam War snipers wear diapers?
Snipers often stayed hidden for several days without moving a muscle.
Even the smallest shift in position could expose them to enemy patrols.
To avoid giving away their location, snipers wore special diapers that resisted heat, itching, and odor—allowing them to remain completely motionless.
In the darkness of the jungle, this simple but uncomfortable tool became essential for survival.
#MilitaryHistory #Snipers #VietnamWar

snippet.title: Persia or Iran? Farsi or Persian? Which one is right?
snippet.description:
The country of Iran used to be called Persia. Who changed its name and why? Also is the language of Iran Persian or Farsi? Is it okay to say "Persian"? Where do the words "Persian" and "Farsi" come from? 

I answer all these questions in this video.

https://web.archive.org/web/20160714205848/http://www.iran-heritage.org/interestgroups/language-article5.htm

N.B.: Don't think that because some Iranians/Persians in the comments are objecting to the terms "Persia" and "Persian", that that represents all people of Iran or of Persian culture. Many Persians would prefer that Westerners use the term "Persian." Some prominent ones are named in the short article linked above, and I have also known Persians in my daily life who expressed this view. When Reza Shah issued that request to foreign governments in 1934, he created an unnecessary complication that makes it more difficult for foreigners to get to know and understand the Persian people.

Sources for my claim that Reza Shah's request was a 'marketing gimmick':

"The most visible name change came in 1934 when Reza Shah -- prompted by his legation in Berlin -- decreed that henceforth Persia was to be known to the outside world as Iran. A government circular explained that whereas "Persia" was associated with Fars and Qajar decadence, "Iran" invoked the glories and birthplace of the ancient Aryans." 
Ervand Abrahamian, A History of Modern Iran (Cambridge, 2009), page 86

"In terms of foreign policy, Reza Shah was determined to maintain Iran's independence and to restore its sense of national pride by elevating its stature in the world and insisting it be treated with respect. This was the motivation behind any number of his actions, from insisting on the use of the name Iran instead of Persia to banning photographs of things that were picturesque but might give an impression of backwardness (camels, for example) to breaking off diplomatic relations with countries if its newspapers published unflattering articles about him or his country."
Elton L. Daniel, The History of Iran (Greenwood Press, 2001), pages 139-140

It became one of the most dangerous and legendary guerrilla tactics of the entire war.

snippet.title: How Medieval Peasants Cooked Without Kitchens
snippet.description:
When you picture cooking, you probably imagine a full kitchen but for most medieval peasants, that simply didn’t exist. Meals were prepared using basic tools, open fires, and shared spaces, often with very limited equipment.

In this video, we explore how ordinary people managed to cook daily meals without modern kitchens, using simple setups that were practical, efficient, and surprisingly effective.

You’ll Discover:
How open hearths were used for boiling, roasting, and baking
The role of communal ovens in villages
Simple tools like pots, spits, and cauldrons
How food was prepared with minimal space and resources
Why cooking methods were built around fire and availability

No stoves. No countertops. No appliances. Just fire, skill, and resourcefulness.

Sometimes the simplest setups… fed entire communities.

snippet.title: A second chance to breathe #art #SecondChance #Automata #Rebirth
snippet.description:
British artist Tim Lewis transforms discarded objects into living creatures. In "The Forest Visits," thrown-away Christmas trees become hybrid animals with heads of echidnas.

His sculptures don't move on their own. They wait until someone engages—a crank, a lever, a moment of attention. Then they breathe.

Lewis sees no boundary between nature and machine. As he puts it: birds build nests, termites build mounds, and we build our world. His creatures blur the line between organic and mechanical.

The message: Nothing is truly finished. Everything deserves a second chance.

snippet.title: Why Soviet Soldiers Slept Sitting Against Trees?
snippet.description:
Soviet winter survival, Eastern Front cold, WWII Russian soldiers — the shocking reason they slept sitting against trees in −40°C.How freezing ground, snow, and enemy patrols forced Soviet troops into an unusual and dangerous sleeping method.On the Eastern Front, the ground was so cold that lying down could lead to hypothermia in minutes.To stay alive, Soviet soldiers slept sitting upright with their backs against trees to avoid touching the frozen earth.
This posture helped them conserve heat and react instantly if German patrols approached.
In the brutal Soviet winter, sleeping the wrong way was often more dangerous than enemy bullets.
#worldwar2 #militaryhistory

snippet.title: The Forgotten Material That Protected Medieval Homes From the Cold
snippet.description:
Long before modern insulation, central heating, or double-glazed windows, medieval people discovered clever ways to keep their homes warm through harsh winters. ❄️🏠

In this video, we explore the forgotten material that helped protect medieval houses from freezing temperatures. Used by peasants and townsfolk alike, this simple yet effective resource provided insulation, reduced drafts, and made life far more bearable during the coldest months of the year.

This video respectfully explores the practical ingenuity of medieval builders and homeowners, revealing how everyday materials played a crucial role in survival long before modern technology.

In this video, discover how:
• Medieval homes stayed warm without modern insulation
• Natural materials helped block cold winds and moisture
• Families adapted their houses for harsh winter conditions
• Simple building techniques improved comfort and survival
• Traditional methods influenced home construction for centuries

If you enjoy medieval history, historical engineering, survival skills, and forgotten technologies, this video offers a fascinating look at how people endured winter in the Middle Ages.

snippet.title: He found something inside his body #selfacceptance #art #creepy #paperart
snippet.description:
At age 12, Alex Eckman-Lawn underwent spinal surgery that left him with a metal rod fused to his spine. The experience fundamentally changed how he saw his own body - transforming it from home into prison.

Now, through his haunting multi-layered paper collages using vintage medical texts, he cuts deeper and deeper into anatomical imagery, searching for what's trapped inside. His dimensional artworks create portals that draw viewers into mysterious depths, each layer revealing something hidden beneath.

But what he discovered through years of artistic excavation was more profound than he expected. Sometimes the thing we're trying to escape from is the very thing we need to accept.

snippet.title: The boring truth about the Library of Alexandria
snippet.description:
Modern writers make different claims about who destroyed the Library of Alexandria. Some blame Julius Caesar while others blame a Christian mob or the invading Arabs. But who is really responsible for the Library's demise?

Check out Al Muqaddimah's video: https://youtu.be/ZxwaSMfD8ho

Support my work on Patreon at https://www.patreon.com/premodernist

The image used in the thumbnail and chapter titles is "Incendie Alexandrie" by Hermann Goll, 1876 (https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Incendie_Alexandrie_by_Hermann_Goll_1876.jpg)

1:56 Two libraries
3:49 The Museum
4:25 Peaked in the 200s BC
5:15 Decline
8:55 Papyrus
10:36 Julius Caesar
16:05 The Serapeum
20:46 Muslims
21:08 Three points

FOOTNOTES

 [1] For a reality check on what we do and don't know about the Library of Alexandria, see Roger S. Bagnall, “Alexandria: Library of Dreams,” Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 146, no. 4 (December 2002), 348–62. On the methods of acquiring books, see also S. Johnstone, “A New History of Libraries and Books in the Hellenistic Period,” Classical Antiquity 33, no. 2 (October 2014), 364–65.

[2] Bagnall, “Alexandria: Library of Dreams,” 351–56; Diana Delia, “From Romance to Rhetoric: The Alexandrian Library in Classical and Islamic Traditions,” American Historical Review 97, no. 5 (December 1992), 1458–59.

[3] The location of the Museum is not known for certain, other than that it was part of the palace complex and close to the harbor: P. M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 3 vols. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1972), 1:15; Delia, “From Romance to Rhetoric,” 1450. On ancient museums as temples to the Muses: Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:312–13.

[4] Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:315.

[5] Johnstone, “A New History of Libraries.”

[6] Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:318–19, 333–35.

[7] Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:86.

[8] Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:85.

[9] Bagnall, “Alexandria: Library of Dreams,” 358–59.

[10] The view that Caesar's fire did not affect the Museum Library is based in part on the phrase “storerooms of books” in Cassius Dio (42.38). However, see Hendrickson's comments in “The Serapeum: Dreams of the Daughter Library,” Classical Philology 111, no. 4 (2016), 460–61.

[11] Plutarch, Caesar 49.3; Gellius, Attic Nights 7.17.3.

[12] Strabo describes the Museum at 17.1.8.

[13] Lionel Casson, Libraries in the Ancient World (New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press, 2001), 47; Bagnall, “Alexandria: Library of Dreams,” 357–58; Hendrickson, “The Serapeum,” 461.

[14] For an introduction to the Serapeum, see Hendrickson, “The Serapeum.”

[15] Orosius says the book chests were emptied but doesn't say what happened to the books (Histories against the Pagans 6.15.32).

Bagnall, “Alexandria: Library of Dreams,” Proceedings of the American Philosophical Society 146, no. 4 (December 2002), 348–62. On the methods of acquiring books, see also S. Johnstone, “A New History of Libraries and Books in the Hellenistic Period,” Classical Antiquity 33, no. 2 (October 2014), 364–65.

[2] Bagnall, “Alexandria: Library of Dreams,” 351–56; Diana Delia, “From Romance to Rhetoric: The Alexandrian Library in Classical and Islamic Traditions,” American Historical Review 97, no. 5 (December 1992), 1458–59.

[3] The location of the Museum is not known for certain, other than that it was part of the palace complex and close to the harbor: P. M. Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 3 vols. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1972), 1:15; Delia, “From Romance to Rhetoric,” 1450. On ancient museums as temples to the Muses: Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:312–13.

[4] Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:315.

[5] Johnstone, “A New History of Libraries.”

[6] Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:318–19, 333–35.

[7] Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:86.

[8] Fraser, Ptolemaic Alexandria, 1:85.

[9] Bagnall, “Alexandria: Library of Dreams,” 358–59.

[10] The view that Caesar's fire did not affect the Museum Library is based in part on the phrase “storerooms of books” in Cassius Dio (42.38). However, see Hendrickson's comments in “The Serapeum: Dreams of the Daughter Library,” Classical Philology 111, no. 4 (2016), 460–61.

[11] Plutarch, Caesar 49.3; Gellius, Attic Nights 7.17.3.

[12] Strabo describes the Museum at 17.1.8.

[13] Lionel Casson, Libraries in the Ancient World (New Haven, Conn.: Yale University Press, 2001), 47; Bagnall, “Alexandria: Library of Dreams,” 357–58; Hendrickson, “The Serapeum,” 461.

[14] For an introduction to the Serapeum, see Hendrickson, “The Serapeum.”

[15] Orosius says the book chests were emptied but doesn't say what happened to the books (Histories against the Pagans 6.15.32).

snippet.title: This ONE Winter Choice Decided Who Lived
snippet.description:
One wrong decision. One night without firewood. One sip of icy water. In today's world, we rarely think about the little things, but in the harsh winters of medieval times, a single choice could have sealed the fate of humanity.

 In this video, we'll explore the most formidable enemy of humanity before the invention of antibiotics - winter. And how it divided people into the living and the dead. It's not just about wearing a warm coat. It's all about strategy, foresight, and the fateful decisions our ancestors made every day.

snippet.title: The Tedious Art of Stop Motion #Animation #Art #Creative
snippet.description: This is the patient magic of stop motion. Discover the work of artist Clifford Beddy, who brings charming characters to life using simple clay and felt. Behind every second of fluid animation are hours of meticulous, painstaking work, moving the character one single frame at a time. It's a look at the incredible effort required to make art that feels so effortlessly alive.

snippet.title: The Artist Who Painted Music  #art  #history
snippet.description:
He didn't see the world like everyone else. Wassily Kandinsky had synesthesia - a condition that made him "hear" colors and "see" music. His paintings were actually musical compositions in visual form.

snippet.title: The Finnish Snowman Soldier Myth
snippet.description:
Finnish Winter War myths, WWII camouflage tactics, snowman sniper legend — the strange story of a soldier hiding inside a hollow snowman.
Did Finnish troops really ambush Soviet convoys from inside frozen decoys? The truth is surprising.

During World War II, a popular myth claimed that a Finnish soldier hid himself — and his MP40 — inside a hollowed-out snowman.
After covering it with snow, he and his comrades supposedly waited for days until Soviet troops approached.
The legend says they opened fire from the snowman, destroying an entire convoy.
But historians agree this was just a story; Finnish forces had far more effective winter concealment tactics, such as snow pits, white cloaks, and forest blinds.
#worldwar2 #militaryhistory

snippet.title: How Guards Survived Freezing Nights on Castle Walls
snippet.description:
Medieval guard duty wasn't just about gleaming armor and heroic battles. It was, above all, grueling routine and a fight for survival in extreme conditions. How did sentries manage not to freeze to death while standing on wind‑swept parapets through long winter nights? Did they have secret methods that history textbooks never mention?

Step into the harsh reality of the men who defended the castle at the cost of their own comfort—and sometimes their health.

snippet.description:
What if you knew everything? 🤯 Imagine having the answers to every question, every secret, and every mystery in the universe. Would you use this ultimate knowledge to save the world, or would it become an overwhelming burden?

In this thought-provoking scenario, we explore what life would be like with unlimited knowledge. Could you handle the truth, or would it change you forever?
